validity.researcher_notes: Capacity of 12 bcm per year is backed by the Georgian state gas company, while a 2023 Neftegaz article gives 1.8 bcm per year for the same system. The two figures differ by a factor of about seven, so a person should decide which one applies to this section. Length is blank and no citation gives a length for this section. Several citations describe the Russia to Georgia leg that is already a separate row, P5875.

validity.recommendation: Check Capacity. The sheet has 12 bcm/y from the Georgian state gas company, and a May 2023 Neftegaz article gives a design capacity of 1.8 bcm/y for the same pipeline.
validity.researcher_notes: The Georgian figure is a design throughput for the North-South main pipeline. The Neftegaz figure is stated as design capacity for the Russia to Armenia trunk. Neither is stated for the Tbilisi to Yerevan section by name.

verifications.note: Page states the North-South main gas pipeline design throughput is 12 bcm per year and that the Georgian section is operated by the Georgian Gas Transportation Company. Page does not name the Tbilisi-Yerevan section.

fills.researcher_notes: The Georgian state gas company page on natural gas states a design throughput of 12 billion cubic meters a year for the North-South main pipeline, which is the Georgian name for the trunk that carries Russian gas through Georgia to Armenia. The page names the North-South main pipeline and not the Tbilisi to Yerevan section, so this is a trunk figure that matches the sheet value. A May 2023 Neftegaz article gives a design capacity of 1.8 billion cubic meters a year for the same system, which disagrees. The sheet value stays and the disagreement is filed as a concern.

verifications.note: Table row for the Mozdok-Tbilisi trunk gives 1400,1200 and 500,700 mm, 271 km, 5.4 MPa. Section Tbilisi-Yerevan is not named separately.

fills.researcher_notes: A table of main gas pipelines from a Ukrainian gas transmission operator lists the North Caucasus to Transcaucasia trunk, labeled Mozdok to Tbilisi, with diameters 1400 and 1200 mm on the Russian side and 500 and 700 mm on the other side. Together these match the sheet list of 500, 700, 1200 and 1400 mm. The table names Mozdok to Tbilisi and not Tbilisi to Yerevan, so it supports the list for the trunk as a whole and not for this section alone. Page read as a 2022 Wayback capture.

No harvested citation gives a length for this section. The 2023 Neftegaz article gives section lengths by country of 137 km in Russia, 263 km in Georgia and 212.5 km in Armenia. The Georgian state gas company gives 234 km and, on its project page, 221 km. These figures disagree with each other, and none is the Tbilisi to Yerevan length. The value stays blank. Not searched beyond the wiki citations this pass.

No harvested citation names the operator of this section. The Georgian state company page says the Georgian Gas Transportation Company operates the North-South main pipeline in Georgia, and the 2023 Neftegaz article says Gazprom Armenia operates the Armenian system. The row spans both countries, so neither name fits the whole row. Left blank for a person to decide. Not searched beyond the wiki citations this pass.

verifications.note: States the North Caucasus-Transcaucasia main pipeline was commissioned in 1988; gives country section lengths and a design capacity of 1.8 bcm per year.

fills.researcher_notes: A May 2023 Neftegaz article says the North Caucasus to Transcaucasia main pipeline was commissioned in 1988. This matches the sheet value. The statement is about the whole system and not about the Tbilisi to Yerevan section by name. A 2021 trade journal article dates the older Mozdok to Tbilisi line to 1965, and the Georgian state company says the system was built in the 1960s and 1980s. The 1988 date therefore most likely marks the later Armenian leg. Page read as a Wayback capture.
